text: Preface & Executive Summary

title: Benchmarking Loss Functions for Electrocardiogram Reconstruction
text:
Motivation & Clinical Context
Electrocardiogram (ECG) reconstruction aims to estimate a complete 12-lead ECG representation from a reduced subset of leads—such as a single wearable-like Lead I or a 3-lead input. Mean Squared Error (MSE) is a standard objective, but conditional averaging can attenuate morphology when the missing signal is not uniquely determined by the observed leads. This handbook tests that concern rather than assuming it.

The Regression-to-the-Mean Failure (Presacan et al., 2025)
In Communications Medicine (Nature Portfolio), Presacan et al. (2025) demonstrated that neural networks trained exclusively on MSE suffer from regression to the mean. Because high-amplitude QRS peaks and low-amplitude P-waves are relatively rare across temporal sequences, MSE loss incentivizes the model to output population-average waveforms.
Potential failure modes include P/T delineation error, ST-segment attenuation, and QT/QTc drift. These are hypotheses requiring artifact-backed evaluation; the book does not infer patient harm from synthetic waveforms or global similarity metrics.
       MSE Loss (Regression to Mean)          Combinatorial Composite Loss (Ours)
    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Flat P-waves / Flattened ST    │      │  Candidate shape preservation  │
    │  Damped Peak Amplitudes         │  vs  │  QTc/VCG metrics require audit │
    │  Metrics requiring audit        │      │  No assumed clinical benefit   │
    └─────────────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────────────┘

title: Benchmarking Loss Functions for Electrocardiogram Reconstruction
text:
How to read this handbook
The book begins with evidence, not demonstrations. 1  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics audits the actual local PTB-XL and EchoNext cohorts: record and patient counts, split integrity, label support, missingness, signal shape, units, clipping, lead dependence, and resampling. 2  Dataset Atlas: LUDB, ISP, and Sunnybrook then establishes what LUDB, ISP, and Sunnybrook contribute that the development cohort cannot. Only after those measurement contracts are visible does 3  Preprocessing, Resampling, and Real PTB-XL Dataset Construction explain the preprocessing and wearable-input transformations.
The remaining parts follow the causal order of the study:

Data, cohorts, and measurement — what was observed, how records were partitioned, and which claims each dataset can support.
Reconstruction models and objectives — the architectures and loss terms applied to those inputs.
Clinical and statistical evaluation — paired morphology, delineation, agreement, fairness, robustness, and uncertainty.
Benchmark and external validation — the locked 48-cell evidence, the still-training mixed-level factorial study, device transfer, and EchoNext classifier preservation.

This order is deliberate. A model ranking is uninterpretable until the reader knows the units, split boundary, repeated-patient structure, endpoint prevalence, and downstream measurement contract. Synthetic examples remain in the book as executable tutorials, but they are labeled as demonstrations and never substitute for cohort evidence.

Open this rendered index.html, then use the persistent sidebar or the Previous/Next controls. The four parts and all chapters are members of one Quarto book; tables, figures, equation numbers, citations, and section references share one navigation structure.

section: 1.2 PTB-XL: observed cohort and split contract
text:
1.2 PTB-XL: observed cohort and split contract
The local metadata contain 21,799 ECG records and 28 columns. The ten official stratification folds are nearly balanced (2,173–2,198 records each). The locked model registry maps folds 1–8 to training (17,418 records), fold 9 to validation (2,183), and fold 10 to test (2,198). The registry also reports 1,904 unique patients in the test set, so patient-clustered uncertainty is necessary: record-level resampling would treat repeated ECGs from the same person as independent.
The raw age field deserves an explicit validity audit. Its observed maximum is 300, which is not physiologically plausible as years and should not silently enter subgroup analysis. Age-based EDA must therefore report invalid-value counts and either use a documented correction supplied by the dataset or mark those values missing. It must not “fix” them by clipping without a sensitivity analysis.


Code
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

ROOT = Path("..")
ptb = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/ptb_xl/ptbxl_database.csv")

ptb_audit = pd.DataFrame({
    "quantity": [
        "records", "unique patients", "male-coded (sex=0)",
        "female-coded (sex=1)", "age missing", "age outside [0,120]",
        "fold-10 test records", "fold-10 unique patients"
    ],
    "value": [
        len(ptb), ptb.patient_id.nunique(), (ptb.sex == 0).sum(),
        (ptb.sex == 1).sum(), ptb.age.isna().sum(),
        (~ptb.age.between(0, 120)).sum(), (ptb.strat_fold == 10).sum(),
        ptb.loc[ptb.strat_fold == 10, "patient_id"].nunique()
    ]
})

1.2.1 Leakage checks that must precede modeling

Patient separation: intersect patient IDs across train, validation, and test. Every intersection must be empty.
File inventory: confirm every metadata row resolves to exactly one waveform tensor in its assigned split.
Duplicate signals: hash waveform bytes after canonical dtype conversion. Metadata uniqueness alone cannot detect copied signals.
Label derivation: parse scp_codes deterministically and version the superclass mapping.
Preprocessing fit scope: any learned mean, variance, clipping threshold, or calibration parameter must be fit on training data only.

1.2.2 PTB-XL demographic and diagnostic composition
The next audit separates record counts from patient counts, treats ages outside 0–120 as missing, and derives diagnostic superclasses from the local scp_statements.csv mapping. Superclass counts are multilabel record counts, so their sum can exceed the number of ECGs.


Code
import ast

ptb["analysis_split"] = np.select(
    [ptb.strat_fold <= 8, ptb.strat_fold == 9, ptb.strat_fold == 10],
    ["train", "validation", "test"],
    default="unassigned",
)
ptb["age_valid"] = ptb.age.where(ptb.age.between(0, 120))
ptb_demographics = ptb.groupby("analysis_split").agg(
    records=("ecg_id", "size"),
    patients=("patient_id", "nunique"),
    valid_age=("age_valid", "count"),
    age_median=("age_valid", "median"),
    age_q1=("age_valid", lambda x: x.quantile(0.25)),
    age_q3=("age_valid", lambda x: x.quantile(0.75)),
    male_coded_records=("sex", lambda x: (x == 0).sum()),
    female_coded_records=("sex", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
)

scp = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/ptb_xl/scp_statements.csv", index_col=0)
diagnostic_map = scp.loc[
    scp.diagnostic == 1, "diagnostic_class"
].dropna().to_dict()
superclass_rows = []
for row in ptb[["analysis_split", "scp_codes"]].itertuples(index=False):
    codes = ast.literal_eval(row.scp_codes)
    classes = sorted({
        diagnostic_map[code] for code in codes if code in diagnostic_map
    })
    superclass_rows.extend(
        {"split": row.analysis_split, "superclass": label}
        for label in classes
    )
superclass_counts = (
    pd.DataFrame(superclass_rows)
      .groupby(["split", "superclass"]).size()
      .rename("records").reset_index()
)
print(f"Metadata source: {(ROOT / 'data/ptb_xl/ptbxl_database.csv').resolve()}")
print("Split-level demographics")
display(ptb_demographics)

1.2.3 Executed PTB-XL waveform audit
The following block reads the actual paired WFDB records named by filename_hr and filename_lr in data/ptb_xl/ptbxl_database.csv. To keep HTML rendering reproducible and bounded, it uses a fixed, fold-stratified audit sample of 25 records from each official fold (250 records total); this is an EDA sample, not an inferential subsample. Primary signal summaries use the stored 500 Hz physical waveforms. The paired 100 Hz releases are upsampled to quantify what a 100→500 Hz adapter can and cannot recover.


Code
import wfdb
from scipy.signal import resample_poly, welch

PTB_ROOT = (ROOT / "data/ptb_xl").resolve()
audit_rows = (
    ptb.groupby("strat_fold", group_keys=False)
       .sample(n=25, random_state=20260731)
       .sort_values(["strat_fold", "ecg_id"])
)
signals_hr = []
signals_lr_up = []
for row in audit_rows[["filename_hr", "filename_lr"]].itertuples(index=False):
    signal_hr, fields_hr = wfdb.rdsamp(str(PTB_ROOT / row.filename_hr))
    signal_lr, fields_lr = wfdb.rdsamp(str(PTB_ROOT / row.filename_lr))
    if fields_hr["fs"] != 500 or signal_hr.shape != (5000, 12):
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected PTB-XL high-resolution contract: {row.filename_hr}")
    if fields_lr["fs"] != 100 or signal_lr.shape != (1000, 12):
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected PTB-XL low-resolution contract: {row.filename_lr}")
    if fields_hr["sig_name"] != fields_lr["sig_name"]:
        raise ValueError(f"Lead-order mismatch: {row.filename_hr} vs {row.filename_lr}")
    signals_hr.append(signal_hr.astype(np.float32))
    signals_lr_up.append(
        resample_poly(signal_lr, up=5, down=1, axis=0).astype(np.float32)
    )
ptb_wave = np.stack(signals_hr)  # records × 5000 samples × leads
ptb_lr_up = np.stack(signals_lr_up)
fields = fields_hr
lead_names = fields["sig_name"]

finite = np.isfinite(ptb_wave)
lead_sd = ptb_wave.std(axis=1)
freq, psd = welch(ptb_wave, fs=500, axis=1, nperseg=1024)
band_power = {
    "baseline_<0.5Hz": np.trapz(psd[:, (freq < 0.5), :], freq[freq < 0.5], axis=1),
    "cardiac_0.5-40Hz": np.trapz(
        psd[:, (freq >= 0.5) & (freq <= 40), :],
        freq[(freq >= 0.5) & (freq <= 40)], axis=1
    ),
    "high_40-150Hz": np.trapz(
        psd[:, (freq > 40) & (freq <= 150), :],
        freq[(freq > 40) & (freq <= 150)], axis=1
    ),
}

ptb_signal_audit = pd.DataFrame({
    "lead": lead_names,
    "finite_percent": 100 * finite.mean(axis=(0, 1)),
    "p01_mV": np.quantile(ptb_wave, 0.01, axis=(0, 1)),
    "median_mV": np.median(ptb_wave, axis=(0, 1)),
    "p99_mV": np.quantile(ptb_wave, 0.99, axis=(0, 1)),
    "median_RMS_mV": np.median(np.sqrt(np.mean(ptb_wave ** 2, axis=1)), axis=0),
    "near_flat_records_percent": 100 * (lead_sd < 1e-4).mean(axis=0),
    "median_high_frequency_fraction": np.median(
        band_power["high_40-150Hz"] /
        np.maximum(
            band_power["cardiac_0.5-40Hz"] + band_power["high_40-150Hz"],
            1e-12
        ),
        axis=0
    ),
})
print(f"Loaded {len(ptb_wave)} paired 500 Hz/100 Hz real records from {PTB_ROOT}")

Because 100 Hz data have a 50 Hz Nyquist limit, upsampling cannot restore true 40–150 Hz content present in the 500 Hz release. The paired error above measures the complete adapter discrepancy; final morphology analysis should additionally compare QRS-band power and fiducials before and after any model-specific resampling.


1.2.4 The actual model-input tensor boundary
Raw WFDB EDA is necessary but not sufficient: the reconstruction code does not read WFDB files during training. scripts/train_mcma_3lead.py::PTBXLDataset loads .pt files, expects shape 12 × 5000, appends 120 zeros to reach a pooling-compatible length of 5,120, and selects lead indices [0, 1, 7]—I, II, and V2—as the model input. Targets contain all 12 padded leads. The training loader applies no per-record standardization, filtering, or amplitude clipping.
The following audit is computed over every tensor, not the 250-record raw-waveform sample. To keep routine book renders tractable, scripts/audit_ptbxl_tensors_for_book.py performs the 5 GB sequential scan with the project venv and writes a record-level Parquet plus a JSON summary. Each tensor is loaded through torch.load(..., weights_only=True) and checked for metadata/split alignment, shape, dtype, nonfinite values, flat leads, amplitude, RMS, and SHA-256 of canonical float32 signal bytes.


Code
import torch
import json

TENSOR_AUDIT_ROOT = ROOT / "results/book_eda"
tensor_inventory_path = TENSOR_AUDIT_ROOT / "ptbxl_tensor_inventory.parquet"
tensor_summary_path = TENSOR_AUDIT_ROOT / "ptbxl_tensor_audit_summary.json"
if not tensor_inventory_path.is_file() or not tensor_summary_path.is_file():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "Run with the project venv: "
        "python scripts/audit_ptbxl_tensors_for_book.py"
    )

tensor_inventory = pd.read_parquet(tensor_inventory_path)
tensor_summary = json.loads(tensor_summary_path.read_text())
tensor_gate = pd.DataFrame({
    "gate": [
        "metadata rows matched one-to-one",
        "unexpected or missing split assignments",
        "shape 12 × 5000",
        "dtype float32",
        "records with nonfinite values",
        "records with at least one flat lead",
        "unique canonical signal hashes",
        "duplicate signal-hash groups",
    ],
    "observed": [
        tensor_summary["metadata_tensor_alignment"].get("both", 0),
        tensor_summary["metadata_tensor_alignment"].get("left_only", 0)
        + tensor_summary["metadata_tensor_alignment"].get("right_only", 0),
        tensor_summary["shape_12_by_5000"],
        tensor_summary["float32"],
        tensor_summary["records_with_nonfinite_values"],
        tensor_summary["records_with_flat_leads"],
        tensor_summary["unique_signal_hashes"],
        tensor_summary["duplicate_hash_groups"],
    ],
    "required": [
        tensor_summary["record_count"], 0, tensor_summary["record_count"],
        tensor_summary["record_count"], 0, "review, do not silently drop",
        tensor_summary["record_count"], 0,
    ],
})
print(f"Full tensor inventory: {tensor_inventory_path.resolve()}")
print(f"Audit implementation: {(ROOT / tensor_summary['audit_script']).resolve()}")

The executed gate finds all 21,799 of 21,799 expected tensors in the correct split, all with shape 12 × 5000, dtype float32, finite values, and unique canonical signal hashes. It also finds one concrete quality exception: training ECG 12722 has an exactly zero V5 lead. That record should be retained in the cohort ledger and handled by an explicit quality policy, not silently disappear inside a data loader.
The gate distinguishes three failure classes. A missing tensor is a cohort-definition error; a malformed/nonfinite tensor is a preprocessing error; a duplicate canonical hash is a potential leakage or export error requiring record-level adjudication. A perfectly matched inventory does not by itself prove the correct physical units, so the next two checks inspect the distribution and pair tensors back to the raw 500 Hz waveforms.


1.2.5 Byte-level training corpus identity
Shape, dtype, and record counts do not detect a same-size content replacement. The training contract therefore includes a second manifest that hashes the exact bytes of every .pt file and forms each split root as SHA256(record_id:size:file_sha256\n...).

section: 1.3 EchoNext: population, waveform, and endpoint audit
text:
1.3 EchoNext: population, waveform, and endpoint audit
The local EchoNext metadata table contains 100,000 records and 39 fields. The frozen external test array contains 5,442 × 1 × 2,500 × 12 values. At the declared 250 Hz, each trace spans 10 seconds. The singleton axis is a storage/channel wrapper, not an ECG lead. Lead order is explicitly:
\[[I,II,III,aVR,aVL,aVF,V_1,V_2,V_3,V_4,V_5,V_6].\]
The waveforms are stored as float64 after official per-lead clipping and train-set z-scoring. Evaluation inverts that affine transform back to clipped microvolts before reconstruction inference. This is a critical domain-transfer detail because PTB-XL models expect 500 Hz, 5,000-sample, physical-mV inputs with no per-record normalization. Resampling, unit conversion, axis ordering, and inverse normalization must all be validated independently.
Only the EchoNext test waveform array is present under the local data/echonext/ tree. Train, validation, and no_split waveform distributions therefore cannot be compared from this repository snapshot; their metadata are auditable, but claiming split-wise waveform parity would exceed the available artifact.
The 100,000-row metadata split is 72,475 train, 4,626 validation, 5,442 test, and 17,457 marked no_split. The unsplit records must not be silently added to training: their role is undefined by the local split field. The cohort is 53,581 male and 46,419 female records, with age 18–90 years (median 63; mean 61.18). Acquisition settings are heavily clinical—48,162 inpatient and 31,453 emergency records, compared with 17,194 outpatient and 3,191 procedural records—so this is not a consumer-wearable population sample.
Race/ethnicity counts are 31,013 Hispanic, 29,211 White, 16,461 Black, 3,428 Asian, 7,429 other, and 12,458 unknown. These are record counts rather than unique-patient counts and should not be presented as independent population denominators when patients have repeated ECGs.

1.4 Endpoint prevalence and effective difficulty
The EchoNext classifier evaluates 12 echo-derived structural-heart-disease endpoints on the same 5,442 test records. Prevalence ranges from 0.37% (20 pulmonary-regurgitation positives) to 42.59% (2,318 composite SHD positives). Consequently:

accuracy is misleading for rare endpoints;
AUROC can look respectable while precision remains low;
average precision must be interpreted against prevalence;
F1 at a fixed 0.5 threshold mixes discrimination with calibration and threshold transport;
confidence intervals for the rarest endpoints will be wide even with 5,442 records.

title: 1  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
text:
1.5 Signal-level EDA: what to measure

1.5.1 1. Units and inverse normalization
For each lead \(\ell\), recover clipped microvolts using
\[x_{\mu V,\ell}=z_\ell\sigma_\ell+\mu_\ell.\]
Then convert once to millivolts if the reconstruction model expects mV:
\[x_{mV,\ell}=10^{-3}x_{\mu V,\ell}.\]
A thousand-fold unit error can produce finite tensors and plausible-looking normalized plots while destroying inference. Unit tests should assert known percentile ranges before and after conversion.


1.5.2 2. Clipping occupancy
Compute the fraction of values equal, or numerically close, to each provenance bound by lead. High occupancy indicates censored amplitude tails. Report this because peak-amplitude and ST-deviation errors are then conditional on the released clipping policy.
In the released test tensor, approximately 0.120–0.144% of samples per lead lie at either documented clipping bound. The inverse-normalized microvolt percentiles show clinically meaningful lead heterogeneity: for example, the 0.1st/99.9th percentiles are −102/287 µV in lead I, −369/173 µV in V1, −527/299 µV in V3, and −246/426 µV in V5. A single global clipping range or scale would therefore distort the precordial leads differently.
The rendered audit below independently reads a fixed 256-record sample from the 1.3 GB memory-mapped array, reverses the released affine normalization using PROVENANCE.json, and recomputes signal-validity and lead-law summaries. The full-array values in the table that follows come from the locked audit; the executable sample serves as a regression test that the live local artifact still has the same axes, scaling, and physiologic lead relations.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(20260731)
echo_idx = np.sort(rng.choice(wave.shape[0], size=256, replace=False))
z = np.asarray(wave[echo_idx, 0, :, :], dtype=np.float64)
means = np.asarray(provenance["normalization"]["mean"], dtype=float)
stds = np.asarray(provenance["normalization"]["std"], dtype=float)
echo_uv = z * stds + means

echo_laws = {
    "III-(II-I)": echo_uv[:, :, 2] - (echo_uv[:, :, 1] - echo_uv[:, :, 0]),
    "aVR+(I+II)/2": echo_uv[:, :, 3] + (echo_uv[:, :, 0] + echo_uv[:, :, 1]) / 2,
    "aVL-(I-II/2)": echo_uv[:, :, 4] - (echo_uv[:, :, 0] - echo_uv[:, :, 1] / 2),
    "aVF-(II-I/2)": echo_uv[:, :, 5] - (echo_uv[:, :, 1] - echo_uv[:, :, 0] / 2),
}
echo_live_audit = pd.DataFrame({

1.5.3 3. Lead-law residuals
The limb leads obey approximate linear relations:
\[III \approx II-I,\quad aVR \approx-\frac{I+II}{2},\quad
aVL \approx I-\frac{II}{2},\quad aVF \approx II-\frac{I}{2}.\]
Residual distributions detect lead permutations, polarity errors, scaling inconsistencies, and corrupted records. These are pipeline diagnostics, not targets to “repair” after looking at test performance.
The actual EchoNext test tensor passes a strong version of this check after inverse normalization. Median record-level residual RMSE is 2.34 µV for \(III-(II-I)\), 0.86 µV for \(aVR+(I+II)/2\), 1.53 µV for \(aVL-(I-II/2)\), and 1.41 µV for \(aVF-(II-I/2)\). Corresponding 99th percentiles are 16.57, 7.44, 11.88, and 9.87 µV. These nonzero residuals reflect quantization/clipping and acquisition representation; they also provide empirical tolerances for future pipeline tests. A residual orders of magnitude larger than these references is a red flag for lead or unit corruption.


1.5.4 4. Spectral and morphology distributions
Report per-lead power in prespecified bands (baseline, P/T, QRS, high-frequency), R-peak count, RR variability, QRS width, QT/QTc, peak amplitude, and flatline fraction. Compare distributions before and after resampling. A global Pearson score can conceal loss of high-frequency QRS energy or systematic ST smoothing.


1.5.5 5. Cross-lead dependence
Plot the \(12\times12\) lead correlation matrix and the distribution of record-level condition numbers. Reconstruction difficulty depends on how much missing-lead information is identifiable from observed leads \(I\), \(II\), and \(V_2\) (indices 0, 1, 7 in the locked registry). Strong average correlation does not imply that diagnostically important residual variation is recoverable.

title: 1  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
text:
1.6 Deep reconstruction diagnostics
A useful diagnostic stack separates four questions.








Layer
Question
Minimum outputs




Sample fidelity
Are point amplitudes close?
MAE/MSE, bias, Bland–Altman, peak error


Shape fidelity
Are morphology and timing preserved?
Pearson, derivative error, DTW, delineation deltas


Physiologic consistency
Do leads form a coherent ECG?
Einthoven residuals, VCG trajectory error, interval consistency


Diagnostic utility
Does a frozen model retain predictions?
per-task AUROC/AP/F1, calibration, paired probability drift



Failure analysis should be record based, not figure based. Rank records separately by MSE, missing-lead Pearson, QRS error, ST error, classifier probability drift, and signal-quality score. The intersection and disagreement among those lists reveal different failure modes:

low MSE + poor classifier fidelity: small but task-aligned feature loss;
high MSE + stable classifier output: nuisance amplitude or baseline mismatch;
strong global Pearson + poor QRS correlation: localized depolarization failure;
good morphology + lead-law violation: cross-lead incoherence;
good mean performance + subgroup tail failure: deployment inequity.

title: 1  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
section: 1.7 Statistical design for the factorial benchmark
text:
1.7 Statistical design for the factorial benchmark
The locked experiment is a \(3\times2^4\) design: three architectures crossed with toggles for MSE (E), correlation (C), MMD (M), and derivative loss (D). The 48 cells permit main-effect and interaction estimates; comparing only “MSE” with “full” wastes most of the design.
Use paired patient-cluster BCa intervals because all cells predict the same test patients and some patients contribute multiple records. For each family and endpoint, estimate
\[\Delta_k=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid k=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid k=0]\]
and prespecified two-way interactions. Family-wise morphology tests use the repository’s corrected threshold; exploratory downstream endpoints must be labeled exploratory. The existing results show significant QRS and ST improvements for full-versus-base in all three architecture families, while ECGFounder AUROC changes are not significant. That supports improved morphology without detected diagnostic-utility loss; it is not proof of clinical equivalence.

title: 1  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
text:
1.8 Reproducible audit checklist

Record exact file hashes and waveform shapes.
Assert patient-disjoint splits and stable record order.
Validate axis order, lead order, sampling rate, unit, and duration.
Quantify invalid demographics and structured missingness.
Report endpoint support before any classifier metric.
Preserve rare-task uncertainty; do not hide it in macro averages.
Compare pre/post-resampling spectra and intervals.
Inspect clipping occupancy and lead-law residuals.
Use patient-clustered paired inference.
Publish per-record outputs so tail failures remain inspectable.

title: 2  Dataset Atlas: LUDB, ISP, and Sunnybrook
text:
2.1 Provenance and governance ledger
The local files do not all have the same documentation status. LUDB is the public PhysioNet release v1.0.1, cited as Kalyakulina et al. with DOI 10.13026/eegm-h675, and is distributed under the Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0. Its source states that 200 ten-second ECGs were collected in 2017–2018, annotated by cardiologists, with written consent and institutional review approval. EchoNext is a restricted PhysioNet resource; the local provenance identifies v1.1.1, while the canonical dataset record and version history are available under DOI 10.13026/2j37-ba56. It uses the PhysioNet Restricted Health Data License/Data Use Agreement 1.5.0; its source documents de-identification and IRB-approved retrospective use.
The ISP folder in this repository does not include a citation, version, license, data-use terms, or a source identifier. Its three class meanings and sampling rate therefore remain unknown in this book. Sunnybrook has a local METADATA.json and README but no accompanying license, cohort selection protocol, subject identifiers, consent/ethics statement, or distribution authority. Until those fields are supplied by the data owner, Sunnybrook is a local exploratory transfer set and ISP is a locally present delineation artifact—not a fully provenance-resolved public benchmark.

2.1.1 Reproducible local fingerprints
The following fingerprints identify the exact artifacts read by this book. A tree hash includes each relative path, file size, and file digest, so a renamed, added, removed, or changed record alters the result.


Code
def file_sha256(path, chunk_size=8 * 1024 * 1024):
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as handle:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: handle.read(chunk_size), b""):
            digest.update(chunk)
    return digest.hexdigest()

def tree_sha256(root, patterns):
    files = sorted({
        path for pattern in patterns for path in root.rglob(pattern)
        if path.is_file()
    })
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    total_bytes = 0
    for path in files:
        size = path.stat().st_size
        total_bytes += size
        digest.update(str(path.relative_to(root)).encode())
        digest.update(str(size).encode())
        digest.update(file_sha256(path).encode())
    return len(files), total_bytes, digest.hexdigest()

fingerprints = []
for dataset, root, patterns in [
    ("LUDB", ROOT / "data/ludb", ["*.hea", "*.dat", "*.atr_*", "README", "LICENSE.txt"]),
    ("ISP", ROOT / "data/isp/isp_delineation_dataset", ["*.hea", "*.dat", "*.csv"]),
    ("Sunnybrook", ROOT / "data/sunnybrook_12_lead_ecg_samples", ["*.xml", "*.csv", "*.json", "*.md"]),
]:
    n_files, n_bytes, digest = tree_sha256(root, patterns)
    fingerprints.append({
        "dataset": dataset, "resolved_root": str(root.resolve()),
        "files_hashed": n_files, "bytes_hashed": n_bytes, "sha256_tree": digest,
    })

for name in [
    "echonext_metadata_100k.csv", "EchoNext_test_waveforms.npy", "PROVENANCE.json"
]:
    path = ROOT / "data/echonext" / name
    fingerprints.append({
        "dataset": f"EchoNext: {name}",
        "resolved_root": str(path.resolve()), "files_hashed": 1,
        "bytes_hashed": path.stat().st_size, "sha256_tree": file_sha256(path),
    })

2.2.2 Demographics and diagnoses
The local headers yield 115 male and 85 female records. Age ranges from 11 to 90 years (mean 51.98, median 56). Diagnoses are overlapping free-text statements. Frequent statements include sinus rhythm (143), left ventricular hypertrophy (108), left atrial hypertrophy (102), normal electrical axis (75), left-axis deviation (66), incomplete right bundle-branch block (29), sinus bradycardia (25), and atrial fibrillation (15).

def parse_ludb_header(path):
    text = path.read_text()
    age = re.search(r"#<age>:\s*(\d+)", text)
    sex = re.search(r"#<sex>:\s*([MF])", text)
    statements = [
        line[1:].strip() for line in text.splitlines()
        if line.startswith("#") and not line.startswith("#<") and line[1:].strip()
    ]
    return {
        "age": int(age.group(1)) if age else np.nan,
        "sex": sex.group(1) if sex else "unknown",
        "statements": statements,
    }

2.2.5 Diagnostics LUDB enables
For P, QRS, and T waves, report onset, peak, and offset error by lead. Matching must be beat-aware and limited to a physiologic window; unconstrained nearest-neighbor matching can pair adjacent cycles. Minimum outputs are sensitivity, positive predictive value, median/IQR/95th-percentile timing error, cycle-mismatch rate, error versus wave amplitude, and interval consistency across leads.
A reconstruction can have high sample correlation but erase a low-amplitude P wave or shift its boundary enough to corrupt PR measurement. LUDB is designed to reveal precisely that failure.

2.3 ISP delineation targets

2.3.1 Local data contract
The ISP CSVs contain 403 training and 72 test rows. Each row includes file_name, age, binary sex coding, and a serialized list of (class, onset, offset) intervals. The training split contains 14,148 intervals and the test split 2,558.
Training class counts are 4,312 / 5,048 / 4,788 for classes 0/1/2; test counts are 793 / 900 / 865. Median widths are 116/110/182 samples in training and 114/110/182 in test. The ordering suggests P/QRS/T-like triplets, but the semantic mapping must come from source documentation rather than inference from sequence alone.
The WFDB files are present and link one-to-one to the CSV file_name inside each split. Their headers declare 12 channels, 1,000 samples/s, approximately 9,998–10,000 samples, and a nonstandard unit token mkv. The numerical scale is consistent with microvolt-like values, but the book does not silently relabel mkv as µV without authoritative provenance.

def load_isp(split):
    path = ROOT / "data/isp/isp_delineation_dataset" / f"{split}_isp_delineation_data.csv"
    frame = pd.read_csv(path)
    frame["intervals"] = frame.target.map(ast.literal_eval)
    frame["interval_count"] = frame.intervals.map(len)
    return frame

isp_train = load_isp("train")
isp_test = load_isp("test")

def interval_audit(frame, split):
    lengths = isp_headers.loc[
        isp_headers.split == split
    ].set_index("file_name").samples
    rows = []
    for _, record in frame.iterrows():
        xs = record.intervals
        record_length = int(lengths.loc[record.file_name])
        rows.append({
            "file_name": record.file_name,
            "valid_class": all(x[0] in {0, 1, 2} for x in xs),
            "positive_width": all(x[1] < x[2] for x in xs),
            "within_window": all(0 <= x[1] < x[2] <= record_length for x in xs),
            "sorted": all(xs[j][1] <= xs[j + 1][1] for j in range(len(xs) - 1)),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

The ranked table makes outlier selection algorithmic. ECG010 and ECG008 appear because of their decoded amplitudes, not because they were selected after viewing model performance. They remain in the primary descriptive analysis; robust medians and leave-one-record-out sensitivity should accompany means.
Fully measured limb leads make Sunnybrook valuable for detecting models that exploit algebraic limb-lead identities while failing on independently acquired morphology.


2.4.3 Hyperfeatures and evidence level
The Philips XLI pipeline supplies global heart rate, PR/QRS/QT/QTc and axes; per-lead P/Q/R/S/T amplitudes; P/QRS/T durations; ST onset/midpoint/J+80/end/slope; measured-lead flags; and diagnostic statements. These are machine-derived reference features, not cardiologist-adjudicated truth.
The set includes sinus rhythms, atrial fibrillation/flutter, old inferior MI, chamber/conduction findings, poor R-wave progression, and a mislaced-lead warning. With only 20 records, these are cases for external stress testing, not stable prevalence or broad clinical-effect estimation.


2.4.4 Retained transients and robust analysis
The comprehensive package retains a 20.44 mV V5 transient in ECG010 and a 6.66 mV V4 transient in ECG008 without clipping. Final analyses should report median/IQR and per-record influence alongside means, with an explicitly labeled sensitivity analysis excluding flagged transients. Silent removal would hide a real robustness failure.
Provenance also notes an approximately 18 µV physical Einthoven residual. This is an empirical acquisition reference, not a universal “errors below 18 µV are perfect” threshold: lead-law residual and reconstruction error are different quantities.
Sunnybrook superclass endpoints use non-adjudicated Philips statement proxies. ECGFounder has probability-fidelity evaluation only because compatible 150-task labels are absent. Those qualifications must appear beside every result table, not only in an appendix.

3.0.1 Mathematical & Anatomical Lead Definitions
However, consumer wearable devices (e.g., Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch) only record a single lead—typically Lead I across the wrists. Smartwatch ECG reconstruction maps this single lead (or a 3-lead patch) to the full 12-lead array.
This chapter presents the production PyTorch Dataset pipeline loading the real PTB-XL clinical dataset (data/ptb_xl/), followed by exploratory Fourier frequency analysis, zero-phase digital filtering, and tensor normalization.

section: 3.1 Production PyTorch Dataset: Loading the Real PTB-XL Clinical Cohort
text:
3.1 Production PyTorch Dataset: Loading the Real PTB-XL Clinical Cohort
We construct PTBXLDataset, a production PyTorch Dataset subclass that loads actual 12-lead clinical ECG recordings from data/ptb_xl/tensors/ (21,799 total 10-second records sampled at \(500\text{ Hz}\)).

3.1.1 Step 1: Defining the PyTorch Dataset Class for PTB-XL


Code
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import scipy.signal as signal

class PTBXLDataset(Dataset):
    """
    Production PyTorch Dataset loading the real PTB-XL Clinical Cohort.
    
    Data Directory: data/ptb_xl/tensors/{train, val, test}
    Tensor Shapes:
        full_12_lead: Tensor of shape (12, 5000) representing 10s at 500 Hz
        input_3_lead: Tensor of shape (3, 5000) selecting Leads II, V1, V5
    """
    def __init__(self, data_dir="../data/ptb_xl", split="val"):
        super().__init__()
        self.data_dir = Path(data_dir)
        self.split = split
        self.tensor_dir = self.data_dir / "tensors" / split
        
        # Fallback path if rendering from root or book subfolder
        if not self.tensor_dir.exists():
            self.tensor_dir = Path("data/ptb_xl/tensors") / split
            
        # Discover all precomputed 12-lead .pt files
        self.file_paths = sorted(list(self.tensor_dir.glob("*.pt")))
        if len(self.file_paths) == 0:
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"No PTB-XL tensor files found in {self.tensor_dir}")

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.file_paths)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        # Load real 12-lead clinical tensor of shape (12, 5000)
        full_12_lead = torch.load(self.file_paths[idx], map_location="cpu")
        
        # Select 3 reduced input leads: Lead II (idx 1), V1 (idx 6), V5 (idx 10)
        input_3_lead = full_12_lead[[1, 6, 10], :] 
        
        return input_3_lead, full_12_lead

# Instantiate real PTB-XL Dataset validation split
dataset = PTBXLDataset(split="val")
print(f"==================================================")
print(f"Successfully loaded PTB-XL Validation Cohort!")
print(f"Total Patient Records: {len(dataset):,}")
x_sample, y_sample = dataset[0]
print(f"Input Patch Tensor Shape:  {tuple(x_sample.shape)}  (3 Leads x 5000 Samples)")
print(f"Target 12-Lead Tensor Shape: {tuple(y_sample.shape)} (12 Leads x 5000 Samples)")
print(f"==================================================")

3.1.2 Line-by-Line Code Breakdown for CS Students

Line 26 (self.tensor_dir = self.data_dir / "tensors" / split): Uses Python’s object-oriented pathlib.Path to resolve operating-system-independent paths. The dataset partitions 21,799 records into official folds: train (folds 1-8), val (fold 9), and test (fold 10).
Line 33 (self.file_paths = sorted(...)): Finds all binary .pt PyTorch tensor files. Sorting ensures deterministic indexing across multiple training runs and GPUs.
Line 41 (torch.load(..., map_location="cpu")): Reads the serialized binary tensor into CPU memory. The tensor contains floating-point voltage values measured in millivolts (\(\text{mV}\)) over \(5000\) discrete time steps (\(10.0\text{ seconds}\) at \(500\text{ Hz}\)). ### Interactive 12-Lead Real Patient Signal Viewer

Below, we load a real patient recording from PTB-XL (y_sample) and plot the full \(6 \times 2\) 12-lead array comparing raw potentials against zero-phase Butterworth bandpass filtered signals (\(0.5 - 45\text{ Hz}\)):


Code
lead_names = ['Lead I', 'Lead II', 'Lead III', 'aVR', 'aVL', 'aVF', 
              'V1', 'V2', 'V3', 'V4', 'V5', 'V6']

fig_12real = make_subplots(rows=6, cols=2, subplot_titles=lead_names, shared_xaxes=True)
t_10s = np.linspace(0, 10.0, 5000)

for idx, name in enumerate(lead_names):
    r_idx = (idx // 2) + 1
    c_idx = (idx % 2) + 1
    raw_sig = y_sample[idx].numpy()
    
    # Add raw trace (blue) and filtered trace (emerald)

section: 3.2 Frequency Domain EDA on Real Patient ECG Signals
text:
3.2 Frequency Domain EDA on Real Patient ECG Signals
We analyze the spectral composition of a real PTB-XL patient recording (Lead I) using the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT).

3.2.1 Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) Math
The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) maps a discrete time-domain signal \(x[n]\) of length \(N = 5000\) into its complex frequency spectrum \(X[k]\):
\[X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] \cdot e^{-j \frac{2\pi}{N} k n}, \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1\]
The Power Spectral Density (PSD) measures power per unit frequency: \[P[k] = \frac{1}{N} |X[k]|^2\]
At \(f_s = 500\text{ Hz}\) and \(N = 5000\), the frequency resolution is \(\Delta f = \frac{500}{5000} = 0.1\text{ Hz}\).


Code
# Extract real Lead I signal from first patient record
fs = 500  # Sampling rate = 500 Hz
real_lead_I = y_sample[0].numpy() # Lead I (Index 0): shape (5000,)
t = np.linspace(0, len(real_lead_I) / fs, len(real_lead_I))

# Compute Discrete Fourier Transform
freqs = np.fft.fftfreq(len(real_lead_I), 1 / fs)
fft_vals = np.fft.fft(real_lead_I)
psd = np.abs(fft_vals) ** 2

# Keep positive frequencies up to Nyquist limit (250 Hz)
pos_mask = (freqs > 0) & (freqs < (fs / 2))
freqs_pos = freqs[pos_mask]
psd_pos = psd[pos_mask]

# Create interactive dual-panel Plotly figure
fig_fft = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=2, 
    subplot_titles=("Real PTB-XL Patient Waveform (Lead I)", "Frequency Power Spectrum (PSD)")
)

fig_fft.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=t[:1500], y=real_lead_I[:1500], mode='lines', name='Real ECG Signal', line=dict(color='#38bdf8')), 
    row=1, col=1
)

    go.Scatter(x=freqs_pos, y=10 * np.log10(psd_pos + 1e-10), mode='lines', name='PSD (dB)', line=dict(color='#f43f5e')), 
    row=1, col=2
)

# Highlight QRS frequency band (10-25 Hz)
fig_fft.add_vrect(
    x0=10, x1=25, fillcolor="rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.25)", 
    layer="below", line_width=0, annotation_text="QRS Band", row=1, col=2

section: 3.3 Digital Signal Filtering: Zero-Phase Butterworth Bandpass Filter
text:
3.3 Digital Signal Filtering: Zero-Phase Butterworth Bandpass Filter
To eliminate baseline wander (\(< 0.5\text{ Hz}\)) and muscle noise (\(> 45\text{ Hz}\)) from real patient recordings, we apply a 3rd-order Butterworth Bandpass Filter using zero-phase forward-backward filtering (scipy.signal.filtfilt).

3.3.1 Mathematical Formulation of Butterworth Filter
\[|H(j\omega)|^2 = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_c}\right)^{2n}}\]
Zero-phase filtering eliminates phase distortion \(\tau(\omega) = 0\), ensuring QRS peak timing remains exact.


Code
# Design 3rd order Butterworth bandpass filter (0.5 Hz - 45 Hz)
nyquist = 0.5 * fs
low_cutoff = 0.5 / nyquist
high_cutoff = 45.0 / nyquist

b, a = signal.butter(3, [low_cutoff, high_cutoff], btype='bandpass')

# Apply zero-phase filtering to real patient signal
filtered_lead_I = signal.filtfilt(b, a, real_lead_I)

# Visualize Raw vs Filtered Real Patient Signal
fig_filt = go.Figure()
fig_filt.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=t[:1500], y=real_lead_I[:1500], mode='lines', 
    name='Raw Real Signal (With Baseline Drift)', 
    line=dict(color='#94a3b8', width=1.5), opacity=0.5
))
fig_filt.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=t[:1500], y=filtered_lead_I[:1500], mode='lines', 
    name='Filtered Signal (Zero-Phase 0.5-45 Hz)', 
    line=dict(color='#10b981', width=2)
))

crumbs: 4  Deep Learning Network Architectures for ECG Reconstruction

title: 4  Deep Learning Network Architectures for ECG Reconstruction
text:
4.1.1 1. 1D Cross-Correlation Convolution
For a 1D sequence tensor \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{in} \times L_{in}}\), a 1D convolutional layer with kernel weight tensor \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{out} \times C_{in} \times K}\) computes:
\[y[c_{out}, t] = b[c_{out}] + \sum_{c_{in}=0}^{C_{in}-1} \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} W[c_{out}, c_{in}, k] \cdot x[c_{in}, t \cdot s + k \cdot d - p]\]
where \(K\) is kernel size, \(s\) is stride, \(p\) is padding, and \(d\) is dilation rate.
The output length \(L_{out}\) is given by: \[L_{out} = \left\lfloor \frac{L_{in} + 2p - d(K-1) - 1}{s} + 1 \right\rfloor\]
For ECG signals sampled at \(f_s = 500\text{ Hz}\), a kernel size of \(K = 15\) with padding \(p = 7\) covers a receptive field of \(\frac{15}{500} = 30\text{ ms}\), corresponding precisely to the duration of a typical QRS onset slope.


4.1.2 2. Transposed 1D Convolution (Fractionally Strided Upsampling)
To upsample feature maps in the decoder, Transposed 1D Convolution reverses the spatial reduction of strided convolutions:
\[L_{out} = (L_{in} - 1) \cdot s - 2p + d(K-1) + \text{output\_padding} + 1\]
When \(s = 2\), \(K = 2\), \(p = 0\), the sequence length doubles (\(L_{out} = 2 L_{in}\)), allowing the network to recover fine temporal resolution.

title: 4  Deep Learning Network Architectures for ECG Reconstruction
text:
4.2 1D U-Net Architecture Implementation
The 1D U-Net uses a symmetric contracting encoder path (which compresses temporal resolution while building high-level cardiac feature representations) and an expanding decoder path (which restores sequence length). Residual skip connections concatenate encoder feature maps directly with upsampled decoder features, preventing loss of high-frequency QRS details.
       Encoder (Contracting)                      Decoder (Expanding)
  Input (3, L) ────► [DoubleConv] ───────────────► Cat ─► [DoubleConv] ─► Output (12, L)
                          │                         ▲
                          ▼ MaxPool(2)              │ ConvTranspose(2)
                      [DoubleConv] ───────────────► Cat ─► [DoubleConv]
                          │                         ▲
                          ▼ MaxPool(2)              │ ConvTranspose(2)
                      [DoubleConv] ───────────────► Cat ─► [DoubleConv]
                          │                         ▲
                          └──────► [Bottleneck] ────┘

4.2.1 PyTorch Implementation & Tensor Flow Breakdown


Code
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class DoubleConv1D(nn.Module):
    """
    Two consecutive 1D Conv layers, each followed by BatchNorm and LeakyReLU.
    Preserves sequence length by setting padding = kernel_size // 2.
    """
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=15):
        super().__init__()
        padding = kernel_size // 2
        self.double_conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=kernel_size, padding=padding, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(out_channels),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True),
            nn.Conv1d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=kernel_size, padding=padding, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(out_channels),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.double_conv(x)

class UNet1DECG(nn.Module):
    """
    1D U-Net for 12-Lead ECG Reconstruction.
    
    Args:
        in_channels (int): Number of input leads (e.g., 3 for patch or 1 for Lead I)
        out_channels (int): Number of target leads (12 for full array)
        base_filters (int): Filter count at first layer (doubles each encoder stage)
    """
    def __init__(self, in_channels=3, out_channels=12, base_filters=64):
        super().__init__()
        # Encoder (Contracting Path)
        self.inc = DoubleConv1D(in_channels, base_filters)
        self.down1 = nn.Sequential(nn.MaxPool1d(2), DoubleConv1D(base_filters, base_filters * 2))
        self.down2 = nn.Sequential(nn.MaxPool1d(2), DoubleConv1D(base_filters * 2, base_filters * 4))
        self.down3 = nn.Sequential(nn.MaxPool1d(2), DoubleConv1D(base_filters * 4, base_filters * 8))

        # Bottleneck
        self.bottleneck = DoubleConv1D(base_filters * 8, base_filters * 8)

        # Decoder (Expanding Path with Transposed Convolution)
        self.up1 = nn.ConvTranspose1d(base_filters * 8, base_filters * 4, kernel_size=2, stride=2)
        self.conv_up1 = DoubleConv1D(base_filters * 8, base_filters * 4)

        self.up2 = nn.ConvTranspose1d(base_filters * 4, base_filters * 2, kernel_size=2, stride=2)
        self.conv_up2 = DoubleConv1D(base_filters * 4, base_filters * 2)

        self.up3 = nn.ConvTranspose1d(base_filters * 2, base_filters, kernel_size=2, stride=2)
        self.conv_up3 = DoubleConv1D(base_filters * 2, base_filters)

        # Final 1x1 Spatial Projection to 12 Clinical Leads
        self.outc = nn.Conv1d(base_filters, out_channels, kernel_size=1)

    def forward(self, x):
        # Encoder
        x1 = self.inc(x)        # Shape: (B, 64, L)
        x2 = self.down1(x1)     # Shape: (B, 128, L/2)
        x3 = self.down2(x2)     # Shape: (B, 256, L/4)
        x4 = self.down3(x3)     # Shape: (B, 512, L/8)

        # Bottleneck
        b = self.bottleneck(x4) # Shape: (B, 512, L/8)

        # Decoder Stage 1 (Concatenate with x3)
        u1 = self.up1(b)        # Shape: (B, 256, L/4)
        x = torch.cat([u1, x3], dim=1) # Shape: (B, 512, L/4)
        x = self.conv_up1(x)    # Shape: (B, 256, L/4)

        # Decoder Stage 2 (Concatenate with x2)
        u2 = self.up2(x)        # Shape: (B, 128, L/2)
        x = torch.cat([u2, x2], dim=1) # Shape: (B, 256, L/2)
        x = self.conv_up2(x)    # Shape: (B, 128, L/2)

        # Decoder Stage 3 (Concatenate with x1)
        u3 = self.up3(x)        # Shape: (B, 64, L)
        x = torch.cat([u3, x1], dim=1) # Shape: (B, 128, L)
        x = self.conv_up3(x)    # Shape: (B, 64, L)

        # Output projection
        out = self.outc(x)      # Shape: (B, 12, L)
        return out

title: 4  Deep Learning Network Architectures for ECG Reconstruction
text:
4.4 ResNet-1D Architecture (Residual Bottlenecks)
While U-Net uses skip connections across resolution levels, ResNet-1D introduces residual blocks within each resolution stage: \[\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \{W_i\}) + \mathbf{x}\]
This identity shortcut allows gradients to flow directly through the network during backpropagation, eliminating vanishing gradients when scaling depth.


Code
class ResBlock1D(nn.Module):
    """
    Residual Block for 1D Signal Processing.
    """
    def __init__(self, channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv1d(channels, channels, kernel_size=7, padding=3, bias=False)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm1d(channels)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv1d(channels, channels, kernel_size=7, padding=3, bias=False)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm1d(channels)

    def forward(self, x):
        residual = x
        out = self.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out))
        out += residual  # Identity shortcut addition
        return self.relu(out)

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
text: 5.1 1. Mean Squared Error (MSE / \(L_2\) Distance)
crumbs: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
text:
5.1.1 Mathematical Definition
For a target tensor \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times T}\) and prediction \(\hat{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times T}\):
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}(Y, \hat{Y}) = \frac{1}{B \cdot C \cdot T} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \sum_{c=1}^{C} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( y_{b,c}(t) - \hat{y}_{b,c}(t) \right)^2\]


5.1.2 Analytical Gradient
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}}{\partial \hat{y}_{b,c}(t)} = -\frac{2}{B \cdot C \cdot T} \left( y_{b,c}(t) - \hat{y}_{b,c}(t) \right)\]

Physiological Purpose: Provides global scale and baseline trajectory alignment.
Limitation: Penalizes large deviations quadratically, forcing predictions toward the dataset temporal mean when missing signals are uncertain.
crumbs: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
text:
5.2 2. Pearson Correlation Coefficient Loss

5.2.1 Mathematical Definition
Measures shape similarity invariant to amplitude scale or baseline offset:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Corr}}(Y, \hat{Y}) = 1 - \frac{1}{B \cdot C} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \sum_{c=1}^{C} \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} (y_{b,c}(t) - \bar{y}_{b,c})(\hat{y}_{b,c}(t) - \bar{\hat{y}}_{b,c})}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T} (y_{b,c}(t) - \bar{y}_{b,c})^2 + \epsilon} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T} (\hat{y}_{b,c}(t) - \bar{\hat{y}}_{b,c})^2 + \epsilon}}\]
where \(\bar{y}_{b,c} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} y_{b,c}(t)\) is the temporal mean of lead \(c\), and \(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\) prevents division by zero.

Physiological Purpose: Forces morphological phase alignment (P-wave, QRS, T-wave timing) without getting penalized by voltage scaling differences.
crumbs: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
text:
5.3 3. High-Frequency First Derivative Loss

5.3.1 Mathematical Definition
Penalizes differences in instantaneous slope (discrete first derivative):
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Deriv}}(Y, \hat{Y}) = \frac{1}{B \cdot C \cdot (T-1)} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \sum_{c=1}^{C} \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \left| \big(y_{b,c}(t+1) - y_{b,c}(t)\big) - \big(\hat{y}_{b,c}(t+1) - \hat{y}_{b,c}(t)\big) \right|\]

Physiological Purpose: Preserves sharp, high-frequency R-peak slopes (\(\frac{dV}{dt} > 50\text{ mV/s}\)) that are smoothed out by standard MSE.
crumbs: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
text:
5.4 4. Einthoven Lead Consistency Loss

5.4.1 Mathematical Definition
By Kirchhoff’s voltage law, the bipolar limb leads must satisfy \(II(t) = I(t) + III(t)\) at every sample. The Einthoven consistency loss penalizes algebraic violations in reconstructed limb leads:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Einthoven}}(\hat{Y}) = \frac{1}{B \cdot T} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( \hat{y}_{b, \text{Lead II}}(t) - \big(\hat{y}_{b, \text{Lead I}}(t) + \hat{y}_{b, \text{Lead III}}(t)\big) \right)^2\]

Physiological Purpose: Enforces strict physical limb lead loop closure, preventing spatial drift in the frontal electrical plane.
crumbs: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
section: 5.5 5. Kors Dower Vectorcardiogram (VCG) Spatial Projection Loss
text:
5.5 5. Kors Dower Vectorcardiogram (VCG) Spatial Projection Loss

5.5.1 Mathematical Matrix Derivation
Vectorcardiography (VCG) projects 12-lead ECGs onto a 3D spatial basis \(\mathbf{V}(t) = [X(t), Y(t), Z(t)]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times T}\), representing orthogonal cardiac electromotive dipole vectors: - \(X(t)\): Transverse vector (Right \(\to\) Left). - \(Y(t)\): Frontal vector (Head \(\to\) Foot). - \(Z(t)\): Sagittal vector (Front \(\to\) Back).
Using the transformation matrix \(\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 12}\):
\[\mathbf{V}(t) = \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{Y}(t)\]
\[\mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix}
-0.172 & -0.074 & 0.122 & 0.231 & 0.239 & 0.194 & 0.156 & -0.010 & -0.089 & -0.215 & 0.010 & 0.000 \\
0.057 & -0.019 & -0.106 & -0.022 & 0.041 & 0.048 & -0.227 & 0.887 & 0.057 & -0.061 & 0.000 & 0.000 \\
-0.229 & -0.310 & -0.017 & -0.021 & -0.025 & 0.063 & 0.022 & 0.102 & 0.513 & 0.387 & 0.000 & 0.000
\end{bmatrix}\]
The VCG spatial loss minimizes 3D spatial trajectory error:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VCG}}(Y, \hat{Y}) = \frac{1}{B \cdot 3 \cdot T} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \left\| \mathbf{D} Y_b - \mathbf{D} \hat{Y}_b \right\|_F^2\]
crumbs: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
text:
5.6 6. Energy Difference (ED) Loss

5.6.1 Mathematical Definition
To combat variance shrinkage, Energy Difference regularizes total signal energy (\(L_2\) norm):
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{ED}}(Y, \hat{Y}) = \frac{1}{B \cdot C} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \sum_{c=1}^{C} \left| \sum_{t=1}^{T} y_{b,c}(t)^2 - \sum_{t=1}^{T} \hat{y}_{b,c}(t)^2 \right|\]

Physiological Purpose: Ensures the total electrical power of reconstructed waves matches ground truth, preventing peak amplitude flattening.

title: 5  Loss Function Formulations & Mathematical Derivations
text:
5.7 7. Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) Kernel Loss

5.7.1 Mathematical Derivation via RKHS Mean Embeddings
Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) measures the distance between two probability distributions \(P\) (ground-truth ECG waveforms) and \(Q\) (reconstructed waveforms) without assuming parametric normality.
Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) equipped with a characteristic feature mapping function \(\phi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H}\) and positive-definite kernel \(k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\).

5.7.1.1 1. Mean Embedding Vector Definition
Every probability distribution \(P\) is mapped to a unique element \(\mu_P \in \mathcal{H}\) called the Mean Embedding:
\[\mu_P \triangleq \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P}[\phi(x)] \in \mathcal{H} \quad \text{satisfying} \quad \langle \mu_P, f \rangle_{\mathcal{H}} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P}[f(x)], \;\;\forall f \in \mathcal{H}\]


5.7.1.2 2. MMD as the Supremum of Function Expectations
MMD is defined as the maximum difference in expectations over all functions \(f\) in the unit ball of \(\mathcal{H}\):
\[\operatorname{MMD}(P, Q) \triangleq \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}} \le 1} \left| \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{y \sim Q}[f(y)] \right| = \|\mu_P - \mu_Q\|_{\mathcal{H}}\]


5.7.1.3 3. Quadratic Expansion with Inner Products
Expanding the squared RKHS norm \(\|\mu_P - \mu_Q\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2 = \langle \mu_P - \mu_Q, \; \mu_P - \mu_Q \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\) yields the sample formula:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{MMD}}^2(P, Q) = \mathbb{E}_{x, x' \sim P}[k(x, x')] + \mathbb{E}_{y, y' \sim Q}[k(y, y')] - 2 \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P, y \sim Q}[k(x, y)]\]
We use a Multi-Scale Gaussian RBF Kernel with bandwidths \(\sigma_m \in \{0.5, 1.0, 2.0\}\) to capture both fine temporal micro-structures (P-wave onsets) and global macro-structures (QRS peaks):
\[k(x, y) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \exp\left( -\frac{\|x - y\|_2^2}{2 \sigma_m^2} \right)\]

text:
5.9 Full PyTorch Combinatorial Loss Implementation


Code
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

class PearsonCorrelationLoss(nn.Module):
    """Pearson Correlation Coefficient Loss."""
    def __init__(self, eps=1e-8):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, pred, target):
        pred_centered = pred - pred.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        target_centered = target - target.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)

        pred_std = torch.sqrt(torch.sum(pred_centered ** 2, dim=-1) + self.eps)
        target_std = torch.sqrt(torch.sum(target_centered ** 2, dim=-1) + self.eps)

        corr = torch.sum(pred_centered * target_centered, dim=-1) / (pred_std * target_std)
        return 1.0 - corr.mean()

class HighFrequencyDerivativeLoss(nn.Module):
    """First derivative slope penalty."""
    def forward(self, pred, target):
        pred_diff = pred[:, :, 1:] - pred[:, :, :-1]
        target_diff = target[:, :, 1:] - target[:, :, :-1]
        return F.l1_loss(pred_diff, target_diff)

class EinthovenConsistencyLoss(nn.Module):
    """Enforces Lead II = Lead I + Lead III."""
    def forward(self, pred):
        # Index 0: Lead I, Index 1: Lead II, Index 2: Lead III
        lead_I = pred[:, 0, :]
        lead_II = pred[:, 1, :]
        lead_III = pred[:, 2, :]
        
        einthoven_err = lead_II - (lead_I + lead_III)
        return torch.mean(einthoven_err ** 2)

class KorsVCGLoss(nn.Module):
    """Kors Dower 3D VCG Projection Loss."""
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # 3x12 Dower Transformation Matrix registered as a non-trainable PyTorch buffer
        dower_mat = torch.tensor([
            [-0.172, -0.074, 0.122, 0.231, 0.239, 0.194, 0.156, -0.010, -0.089, -0.215, 0.010, 0.000],
            [ 0.057, -0.019, -0.106, -0.022, 0.041, 0.048, -0.227, 0.887, 0.057, -0.061, 0.000, 0.000],
            [-0.229, -0.310, -0.017, -0.021, -0.025, 0.063, 0.022, 0.102, 0.513, 0.387, 0.000, 0.000]
        ], dtype=torch.float32)
        self.register_buffer('dower_mat', dower_mat)

    def forward(self, pred, target):
        batch, leads, time = pred.shape
        pred_flat = pred.transpose(1, 2).reshape(-1, leads)
        target_flat = target.transpose(1, 2).reshape(-1, leads)

        # Matrix multiplication to project 12-lead -> 3D VCG (X, Y, Z)
        pred_vcg = torch.matmul(pred_flat, self.dower_mat.T)
        target_vcg = torch.matmul(target_flat, self.dower_mat.T)

        return F.mse_loss(pred_vcg, target_vcg)

class EnergyDifferenceLoss(nn.Module):
    """Regularizes total signal energy norm."""
    def forward(self, pred, target):
        pred_energy = torch.sum(pred ** 2, dim=-1)
        target_energy = torch.sum(target ** 2, dim=-1)
        return F.l1_loss(pred_energy, target_energy)

class CombinatorialCompositeLoss(nn.Module):
    """Master Combinatorial Loss Aggregator."""
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.mse = nn.MSELoss()
        self.corr = PearsonCorrelationLoss()
        self.deriv = HighFrequencyDerivativeLoss()
        self.einthoven = EinthovenConsistencyLoss()
        self.vcg = KorsVCGLoss()
        self.ed = EnergyDifferenceLoss()

    def forward(self, pred, target):
        l_mse = self.mse(pred, target)
        l_corr = self.corr(pred, target)
        l_deriv = self.deriv(pred, target)
        l_einthoven = self.einthoven(pred)
        l_vcg = self.vcg(pred, target)
        l_ed = self.ed(pred, target)

        total_loss = (
            10.0 * l_mse + 
            2.0 * l_corr + 
            5.0 * l_deriv + 
            1.0 * l_einthoven + 
            1.0 * l_vcg + 
            0.5 * l_ed
        )
        return total_loss, {
            "mse": l_mse.item(), "corr": l_corr.item(), 
            "deriv": l_deriv.item(), "einthoven": l_einthoven.item(),
            "vcg": l_vcg.item(), "ed": l_ed.item()
        }

# Verify forward & backward autograd pass
loss_fn = CombinatorialCompositeLoss()
pred_dummy = torch.randn(4, 12, 1000, requires_grad=True)
target_dummy = torch.randn(4, 12, 1000)
loss_val, metrics = loss_fn(pred_dummy, target_dummy)
loss_val.backward()
print("Combinatorial Composite Loss Autograd Gradient Check Passed!")
print(f"Total Loss Value: {loss_val.item():.4f}")

# Plot Gradient Norm Magnitudes per Loss Component
loss_names = list(metrics.keys())
loss_magnitudes = [10.0 * metrics['mse'], 2.0 * metrics['corr'], 5.0 * metrics['deriv'], 
                   1.0 * metrics['einthoven'], 1.0 * metrics['vcg'], 0.5 * metrics['ed']]

fig_grad = go.Figure(data=[go.Bar(
    x=loss_names, y=loss_magnitudes,
    marker_color=['#38bdf8', '#f43f5e', '#10b981', '#fbbf24', '#a855f7', '#ec4899']
)])
fig_grad.update_layout(
    title="Combinatorial Composite Loss Component Gradient Contribution (Weighted Magnitude)",
    xaxis_title="Loss Component",
    yaxis_title="Weighted Loss Magnitude",
    template="plotly_dark",
    height=400, margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=50, b=20)
)
fig_grad.show()

title: 6  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
text:
6.1 Mathematical Formulations of QTc Interval Correction
The QT interval measures the total temporal duration of ventricular depolarization (\(QRS\)) and repolarization (\(T\)-wave). Because QT duration shortens as heart rate increases, clinical interpretation requires calculating the rate-corrected QT interval (QTc).
Let \(\mathrm{QT}\) be the uncorrected interval in seconds and \(\mathrm{RR}\) be the cardiac cycle length (\(R\text{-to-}R\) interval) in seconds:
\[\mathrm{RR} = \frac{60}{\mathrm{HR} \text{ (bpm)}}\]

title: 6  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
text:
6.1.1 1. Bazett Formula (1920)
\[\mathrm{QTc}_B = \frac{\mathrm{QT}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{RR}}}\]

Limitation: Derived empirically from a small cohort. Overcorrects at tachycardia (\(\mathrm{HR} > 80\text{ bpm}\)), leading to false-positive Long QT diagnoses; undercorrects at bradycardia (\(\mathrm{HR} < 60\text{ bpm}\)).



6.1.2 2. Fridericia Formula (1920)
\[\mathrm{QTc}_F = \frac{\mathrm{QT}}{\sqrt[3]{\mathrm{RR}}}\]

Advantage: Substantially reduces heart-rate dependence across normal physiological ranges (\(50 - 120\text{ bpm}\)). Recommended by the FDA for drug-induced repolarization toxicity trials.



6.1.3 3. Framingham Linear Formula (1992)
\[\mathrm{QTc}_{\text{Fram}} = \mathrm{QT} + 0.154 \cdot (1 - \mathrm{RR})\]


6.1.4 4. Hodges Linear Formula (1983)
\[\mathrm{QTc}_{\text{Hodges}} = \mathrm{QT} + 0.00175 \cdot (\mathrm{HR} - 60)\]

title: 6  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
section: 6.2 Bipartite Event Matching & Fiducial Error Assignment
text:
6.2 Bipartite Event Matching & Fiducial Error Assignment
Evaluating delineation error requires pairing ground-truth cardiac events \(R = \{r_i\}_{i=1}^{N}\) with predicted events \(P = \{p_j\}_{j=1}^{M}\) within a maximum temporal tolerance \(\tau = 50\text{ ms}\).

6.2.1 Bipartite Graph Optimization Problem
Find a 1-to-1 matching permutation \(\pi\) that minimizes total timing error:
\[\min_{\pi} \sum_{i} |r_i - p_{\pi(i)}| \quad \text{subject to} \quad |r_i - p_{\pi(i)}| \le \tau\]
Unmatched reference events \(r_i\) are categorized as False Negatives (FN); unmatched predicted events \(p_j\) are False Positives (FP).


6.2.2 Signed Timing Error Definition
For matched event pairs:
\[e_i = 1000 \cdot \frac{p_{\pi(i)} - r_i}{f_s} \quad \text{(in milliseconds, ms)}\]

\(e_i > 0\): Reconstructed wave is delayed relative to ground truth (late detection).
\(e_i < 0\): Reconstructed wave is advanced relative to ground truth (early detection).



6.2.3 QTc Formula Sensitivity Across Heart Rates (40-140 bpm)
Below, we simulate QTc calculations across a range of heart rates (\(40 - 140\text{ bpm}\)) with a fixed QT interval of \(400\text{ ms}\) to compare formula stability:


Code

fig_qtc.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=hr_range, y=qtc_framingham, mode='lines', line=dict(color='#10b981', width=2), name='Framingham Linear Correction'))

title: 6  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
text:
6.3 Automated Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) Delineation
We use Continuous Wavelet Transforms (CWT) with a Mexican Hat mother wavelet \(\psi(t)\) to detect steep wave zero-crossings:
\[\psi(t) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3\sigma} \pi^{1/4}} \left( 1 - \frac{t^2}{\sigma^2} \right) e^{-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]
High-resolution scales isolate sharp QRS spikes (\(10-25\text{ Hz}\)), while lower-resolution scales detect smooth P and T wave peaks (\(1-10\text{ Hz}\)).


Code
import neurokit2 as nk
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# 1. Simulate a 5-second 12-lead ECG signal at 500 Hz

ecg_signal = nk.ecg_simulate(duration=5, sampling_rate=sampling_rate, heart_rate=72)

# 2. Clean signal using zero-phase Butterworth bandpass filter

# 3. Locate R-peaks
_, rpeaks = nk.ecg_peaks(ecg_cleaned, sampling_rate=sampling_rate)

# 4. Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) Delineation for P, Q, S, T boundaries

# Generate time vector in seconds

        ))

text:
6.4 QTc Formula Comparison Function


Code
def calculate_qtc_variations(qt_ms, rr_ms):
    """
    Computes QTc across Bazett, Fridericia, Framingham, and Hodges formulas.
    
    Args:
        qt_ms (float): Uncorrected QT interval in milliseconds.
        rr_ms (float): R-R interval in milliseconds.
    """
    qt_sec = qt_ms / 1000.0
    rr_sec = rr_ms / 1000.0
    hr = 60.0 / rr_sec
    
    qtc_bazett = (qt_sec / np.sqrt(rr_sec)) * 1000.0
    qtc_fridericia = (qt_sec / (rr_sec ** (1/3))) * 1000.0
    qtc_framingham = (qt_sec + 0.154 * (1.0 - rr_sec)) * 1000.0
    qtc_hodges = qt_ms + 1.75 * (hr - 60.0)
    
    return {
        "Heart Rate (bpm)": round(hr, 1),
        "Uncorrected QT (ms)": round(qt_ms, 1),
        "QTc Bazett (ms)": round(qtc_bazett, 1),
        "QTc Fridericia (ms)": round(qtc_fridericia, 1),
        "QTc Framingham (ms)": round(qtc_framingham, 1),
        "QTc Hodges (ms)": round(qtc_hodges, 1)
    }

# Compare QTc corrections at Normal HR (70 bpm) vs Tachycardia (110 bpm)
normal_hr_stats = calculate_qtc_variations(qt_ms=400, rr_ms=857) # 70 bpm
tachy_hr_stats = calculate_qtc_variations(qt_ms=340, rr_ms=545)  # 110 bpm

print("==================================================")
print("Normal Heart Rate (70 bpm) QTc Comparison:")
print(normal_hr_stats)
print("\nTachycardic Heart Rate (110 bpm) QTc Comparison:")
print(tachy_hr_stats)
print("==================================================")

title: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text: 7.1 Mathematical Proof: Why \(L_2\) Minimization Induces Regression to the Mean
crumbs: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean

title: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text:
7.1.1 Theorem 1: \(L_2\) Minimization Yields the Conditional Expectation
Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{in} \times T}\) be the input lead tensor and \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{out} \times T}\) be the target 12-lead tensor with joint probability density \(p(X, Y)\).
Objective: Find a neural network function \(f^*(X)\) minimizing the expected squared error:
\[f^*(X) = \arg\min_f \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y)} \left[ \| f(X) - Y \|_2^2 \right]\]
Proof: Using the law of total expectation, we expand the expected loss:
\[\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)} \left[ \| f(X) - Y \|_2^2 \right] = \mathbb{E}_{X} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{Y|X} \left[ \| f(X) - Y \|_2^2 \;\middle|\; X \right] \right]\]
To minimize the outer expectation, we minimize the inner conditional expectation point-wise for every fixed value of \(X = x\):
\[\mathcal{L}(f(x)) = \int (f(x) - y)^2 \, p(y \mid x) \, dy\]
Differentiating \(\mathcal{L}(f(x))\) with respect to \(f(x)\) and setting the derivative to zero:
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial f(x)} = \int 2 \cdot (f(x) - y) \, p(y \mid x) \, dy = 0\]
\[2 \cdot f(x) \int p(y \mid x) \, dy - 2 \int y \cdot p(y \mid x) \, dy = 0\]
Since \(\int p(y \mid x) \, dy = 1\):
\[f^*(x) = \int y \cdot p(y \mid x) \, dy = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]\]
\(\blacksquare\)



7.1.2 Corollary 1: Variance Shrinkage & Amplitude Attenuation
By the Law of Total Variance:
\[\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\big) + \mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)\big]\]
Since \(\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X) \ge 0\), it follows that:
\[\operatorname{Var}\big(f^*(X)\big) = \operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\big) \le \operatorname{Var}(Y)\]
Equality holds if and only if \(Y\) is a deterministic function of \(X\) (\(\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X) = 0\)). Whenever \(X\) contains incomplete spatial information (e.g., Lead I only), \(\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X) > 0\), forcing:
\[\operatorname{Var}(\hat{Y}) < \operatorname{Var}(Y)\]
Clinical Consequence: \(L_2\) models systematically shrink high-amplitude QRS peaks (\(R\)-waves) toward zero and flatten \(P\)-waves and \(T\)-waves, producing a false “low-voltage” clinical phenotype.



7.1.3 Wasserstein-1 Distance (\(W_1\) Earth Mover’s Metric)
To quantify the total probability mass shift caused by variance shrinkage, we compute the 1D Wasserstein-1 Distance (\(W_1\)) between the empirical cumulative distribution functions \(F_P(u)\) (ground truth) and \(F_Q(u)\) (prediction):
\[W_1(P, Q) \triangleq \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(P, Q)} \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \gamma} \left[ \|x - y\|_1 \right] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left| F_P(u) - F_Q(u) \right| \, du\]
where \(\Pi(P, Q)\) denotes the set of all joint distributions whose marginals are \(P\) and \(Q\).

Physical Interpretation: \(W_1\) measures the minimum “work” (probability mass \(\times\) transport distance) required to transform the predicted peak amplitude distribution \(Q\) into the true physiological distribution \(P\).
\(L_2\) Model vs. MMD Model: An \(L_2\) model produces a large \(W_1\) distance due to probability mass concentration near the mean \(\mu\), whereas MMD regularization forces \(W_1(P, Q) \to 0\).

title: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
section: 7.2 Why Pearson Correlation (\(r\)) Cannot Prove Agreement
text:
7.2 Why Pearson Correlation (\(r\)) Cannot Prove Agreement
A common misconception in model evaluation is using Pearson’s correlation coefficient (\(r\)) to claim reconstruction accuracy. As proved by Giavarina (2015): - Pearson correlation measures linear association, not agreement. - If \(\hat{Y} = 0.5 \cdot Y + 0.1\), the correlation is perfect (\(r = 1.0\)), yet the predicted amplitudes suffer a \(50\%\) clinical loss!
To measure true clinical comparability, we must use Bland-Altman Agreement Analysis.
crumbs: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean

title: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text:
7.3 Advanced Bland-Altman Statistical Battery
Our evaluation battery executes four non-parametric statistical tests:

Mean Bias (\(\bar{d}\)): \[\bar{d} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i, \quad d_i = \hat{y}_i - y_i\]
95% Limits of Agreement (LoA): \[\text{LoA} = \left[ \bar{d} - 1.96 \cdot s_d, \;\; \bar{d} + 1.96 \cdot s_d \right], \quad s_d = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (d_i - \bar{d})^2}\]
Non-Parametric BCa Bootstrap Confidence Intervals (9,999 Resamples): Constructs 95% Confidence Intervals for \(\bar{d}\) without assuming Gaussian errors.
Levene’s Test for Homoscedasticity: Verifies whether error variance \(s_d^2\) depends on peak amplitude magnitude.
crumbs: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean

title: 7  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text:
7.4 Python Implementation: Bland-Altman Statistical Suite


Code
import torch
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from scipy import stats

def compute_ba_statistics(pred_peaks, target_peaks, model_name):
    """
    Computes Bland-Altman agreement statistics: Mean Bias, 95% LoA, 
    BCa Bootstrap 95% CI, Shapiro-Wilk Normality, and Levene Homoscedasticity.
    """
    diff = pred_peaks - target_peaks
    mean_val = (pred_peaks + target_peaks) / 2.0
    
    bias = np.mean(diff)
    std_diff = np.std(diff, ddof=1)
    
    loa_lower = bias - 1.96 * std_diff
    loa_upper = bias + 1.96 * std_diff
    
    # 1. Non-parametric BCa Bootstrap for Bias 95% CI (9,999 resamples)
    res = stats.bootstrap(
        (diff,), np.mean, 
        confidence_level=0.95, n_resamples=9999, method='BCa'
    )
    ci_lower, ci_upper = res.confidence_interval
    
    # 2. Shapiro-Wilk test for normality of differences
    stat_sw, p_value_sw = stats.shapiro(diff)
    normality_msg = "Normal" if p_value_sw > 0.05 else "Non-Normal"
    
    # 3. Levene's Test for Homoscedasticity (Lower half vs Upper half)
    median_val = np.median(mean_val)
    diff_lower = diff[mean_val <= median_val]
    diff_upper = diff[mean_val > median_val]
    stat_lev, p_value_lev = stats.levene(diff_lower, diff_upper)
    levene_msg = "Homoscedastic" if p_value_lev > 0.05 else "Heteroscedastic"
    
    # 4. Percentage bias calculation
    pct_diff = (diff / mean_val) * 100
    pct_bias = np.mean(pct_diff)
    
    print(f"=== {model_name} Bland-Altman Audit ===")
    print(f"Mean Bias (\u0304d): {bias:.4f} mV (BCa 95% CI: [{ci_lower:.4f}, {ci_upper:.4f}])")
    print(f"Limits of Agreement (95% LoA): [{loa_lower:.4f}, {loa_upper:.4f}]")
    print(f"Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test: p = {p_value_sw:.4f} ({normality_msg})")
    print(f"Levene Homoscedasticity Test: p = {p_value_lev:.4f} ({levene_msg})")
    print(f"Percentage Bias: {pct_bias:.2f}%")
    print("-" * 50)
    
    return mean_val, diff, bias, loa_lower, loa_upper, pct_diff, pct_bias

# Simulate N=300 peak amplitudes to demonstrate statistical suite
np.random.seed(42)
target_peaks = np.random.normal(1.2, 0.4, 300)

# 1. Stipulated MSE Model (30% amplitude attenuation factor)
mse_peaks = target_peaks * 0.70 + np.random.normal(0, 0.03 * np.abs(target_peaks), 300)

# 2. Stipulated Combinatorial Model (Preserves 99% peak amplitude)
comp_peaks = target_peaks * 0.99 + np.random.normal(0, 0.02, 300)

(mse_means, mse_diffs, mse_bias, mse_loa_l, mse_loa_u, mse_pct_diff, mse_pct_bias) = compute_ba_statistics(mse_peaks, target_peaks, "MSE Model ($L_2$)")
(comp_means, comp_diffs, comp_bias, comp_loa_l, comp_loa_u, comp_pct_diff, comp_pct_bias) = compute_ba_statistics(comp_peaks, target_peaks, "Combinatorial Loss Model")

title: 8  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
text:
8.1 Signal Quality Index (SQI) Formulations
Signal Quality Indices (SQIs) evaluate whether a recorded or reconstructed ECG is suitable for clinical delineation without requiring ground-truth clean signals.
crumbs: 8  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)

title: 8  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
text:
8.1.1 1. Kurtosis SQI (\(kSQI\))
Kurtosis measures the “peakedness” of the signal amplitude distribution:
\[kSQI = \frac{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^4}{\left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \right]^2}\]

Physiological Basis: Normal clean ECG signals contain sharp QRS spikes, yielding high positive kurtosis (\(kSQI > 5.0\)). Gaussian white noise has \(kSQI \approx 3.0\), while severe baseline wander or flatlines reduce \(kSQI < 2.0\).



8.1.2 2. Skewness SQI (\(sSQI\))
Skewness measures asymmetry around the mean:
\[sSQI = \frac{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^3}{\left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \right]^{3/2}}\]


8.1.3 3. Relative QRS Power Spectral SQI (\(pSQI\))
Measures the proportion of signal power concentrated within the QRS frequency band (\(5 - 15\text{ Hz}\)) relative to the total physiological band (\(5 - 40\text{ Hz}\)):
\[pSQI = \frac{\int_{5}^{15} P(f) \, df}{\int_{5}^{40} P(f) \, df}\]
where \(P(f) = |X(f)|^2\) is the Power Spectral Density obtained via Fast Fourier Transform.
crumbs: 8  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)

title: 8  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
section: 8.2 Noise Stress Testing Mathematics & Noise Models
text:
8.2 Noise Stress Testing Mathematics & Noise Models
To benchmark model robustness, we corrupt clean ECG signals \(x(t)\) with three distinct physical noise models:
\[x_{\text{corrupted}}(t) = x(t) + n_{\text{artifact}}(t)\]

8.2.1 1. Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN)
Noise variance \(\sigma_n^2\) is parameterized by target Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR in dB):
\[\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_{\text{signal}}}{P_{\text{noise}}} \right) \implies \sigma_n = \sqrt{\frac{P_{\text{signal}}}{10^{\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} / 10}}}\]
where \(P_{\text{signal}} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} x(t)^2\).


8.2.2 2. Respiratory Baseline Wander (\(n_{\text{BW}}\))
Simulates low-frequency chest impedance drift caused by respiration (\(0.1 - 0.5\text{ Hz}\)):
\[n_{\text{BW}}(t) = A_{\text{BW}} \cdot \sin(2\pi f_{\text{resp}} t + \phi)\]


8.2.3 3. Electromyographic (EMG) Muscle Tremor Noise (\(n_{\text{EMG}}\))
Modeled as a high-frequency filtered autoregressive process (\(> 35\text{ Hz}\)) simulating random muscle contractions.
crumbs: 8  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)

title: 8  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
text:
8.3 Subgroup Fairness & Disparity Metrics
When evaluating performance across demographic subgroups \(A \in \{\text{Male}, \text{Female}\}\) or age brackets \(A \in \{\text{Age} \le 65, \text{Age} > 65\}\), reporting global aggregate metrics hides disparities.

8.3.1 1. Absolute Performance Disparity (\(\Delta_{\text{perf}}\))
\[\Delta_{\text{perf}} = \text{Metric}(A = \text{Group}_1) - \text{Metric}(A = \text{Group}_2)\]


8.3.2 2. Paired Reconstruction Degradation (\(\Delta_{\text{recon}}\))
Measures the change in metric induced specifically by model reconstruction:
\[\Delta_{\text{recon}}(A_g) = \text{Metric}\big(\hat{Y}_{A_g}\big) - \text{Metric}\big(Y_{A_g}\big)\]
\[\text{Fairness Disparity} = \Delta_{\text{recon}}(\text{Male}) - \Delta_{\text{recon}}(\text{Female})\]
Using patient-clustered non-parametric bootstrapping ensures that repeated recordings from the same patient do not artificially shrink confidence intervals.
